lesson_title: Why Builders Trust the Little Ruler, Not the Ratio
hook_text: That plan says 1 : 50. Photocopy it once and that number is a lie. Here's why the little printed ruler isn't.
clip_script: A plan is just a house that has been shrunk to fit on a page, and the scale is the honest label saying by how much. 1 to 50 means the drawing is fifty times smaller than the real thing — so every centimetre on the paper is fifty centimetres of real wall. Measure the bedroom: 8,4 centimetres. Times 50 is 420 centimetres, which is 4,20 metres. You just measured a room you have never stood in. Page to reality, multiply. Reality to page, divide. But here's the part examiners love asking. Why do plans also carry a little printed ruler next to the ratio? Because a photocopier does not know about ratios. Shrink that page to 80 percent and one to fifty is suddenly a lie — one centimetre no longer means fifty. But the little printed ruler shrank too. It is on the same page, so it stretches and squashes with the drawing, and it stays true at any size. That is why the builder measures against the bar and treats the ratio as a label.
visual_style: A house folding down onto a sheet of paper, a ruler laid along a wall reading 8,4 cm then flipping to 4,20 m; then the page visibly shrinking in a photocopier while the printed bar scale shrinks with it and the '1 : 50' text cracks.
pacing: Brisk measuring demo, dramatic pause at the photocopier, calm confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and price a room's carpet, skirting and paving straight off the plan.
